name: Friendship Bench: talk therapy on the bench (charityevals, 2026)
summary: Friendship Bench trains community health workers, mostly older women, to give problem-solving talk therapy on benches at about 385 clinics across Zimbabwe; in 2024 it saw 295,770 clients for about $3.6 million. Our estimate for 2024 is about 6 years of healthy life per $1,000, with a very wide range. The biggest uncertainty is how much of a full course the average client gets: about 1.75 sessions per client seen against five in the trial that found a very large effect. Research and training abroad (about a tenth of programme spending) aren't modelled, and the Zimbabwe organisation's spending is built from its US affiliate's grant because its own statements aren't published.

resources.title: The Friendship Bench Inc, Form 990 filings (ProPublica)
Chibanda et al. 2016, JAMA: the Friendship Bench trial
Karyotaki et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry: task-shared psychological interventions in LMICs

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Deaths averted, valued the site's way
sections.explainer: Deaths a mental-health program averts (suicides) are valued like every death on the site, in units of value (GiveWell's moral weight for the age band × your value of a life), and enter the WELLBYs only through one fixed row, which the WELLBY unit's conversion cancels: so they don't move with the WELLBY slider (docs/normalization.md 2.3, INV-17).

sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: The US fundraising affiliate has no employees (Form 990: TotalEmployeeCnt 0). Almost all of its spending is a grant to Friendship Bench Zimbabwe (next row); the rest is fees for services ($258,253, of which $209,378 programme services; the return doesn't say what they were for), a $75,000 research grant to the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and small management and fundraising costs.

source.quote: RegionTxt ZIMBABWE; PurposeOfGrantTxt PROGRAM SERVICES; CashGrantAmt 2735000

rows.explainer: Cash sent to Zimbabwe for programme services in 2024 (2023: $2,640,200). The Zimbabwe organisation (a Private Voluntary Organisation audited by Vista Chartered Accountants) does not publish its statements, so its own spending is built from this grant and the share of its money that comes from elsewhere.

rows.label: Share of Friendship Bench Zimbabwe's 2024 spending paid by funders other than the US affiliate
rows.explainer: Friendship Bench Zimbabwe also ran projects funded directly in 2024: the WHO Special Initiative's FRIENDZ scale-up, the Global Fund HIV and mental health integration, USAID's Development Innovation Ventures grant (ended early in 2025) and OPHID's RISE care-for-carers project (annual report 2024, pp. 11–13; the report gives no amounts). Anchor: the US grant ($2.7 million) against the charity's stated need of US$8 million for January 2024 to December 2025, about $4 million a year (annual report 2024, p. 20), which would make others' share about a third if the budget was met in full. 25% best guess, 10% to 40%. The statements themselves would settle it.

rows.label: Friendship Bench Zimbabwe's spending, 2024 (built)
rows.explainer: The US grant grossed up by the share paid by other funders. Context: the charity's 2026 ask is US$4.1 million for 380,000 people (annual report 2025, p. 20); a directory lists its operating budget as $1.1–5 million.

rows.label: Total expenses, 2024 (Friendship Bench Zimbabwe plus the US affiliate's own spending)
rows.explainer: Both organisations together, without counting the grant between them twice: the Zimbabwe organisation's spending plus the US affiliate's spending other than that grant (contracted programme services, a $75,000 research grant, management and fundraising).

rows.label: Management, finance, HR, fundraising and other support costs as a share of total spending

source.title: Friendship Bench, Annual report 2024
source.quote: $3.1M (40%) to Marketing, finance, HR, administration, fundraising costs which underpin programme delivery.

rows.explainer: The charity's own budget for 2024–2025 (US$8 million: $4.9 million, 60%, for programmes; $3.1 million, 40%, for support costs). A budget, not the audited split: the range runs down to 20%, nearer what audited statements of comparable delivery charities show, since budgets presented to donors often put supervision and data systems under support. The US affiliate's own split (2% management and fundraising) covers only its grant-making.

rows.label: Programme expenses, 2024 (all programmes, both organisations)
rows.explainer: Total expenses less support costs, at the charity's budget split.

rows.label: Share of programme spending on talk therapy in Zimbabwe (benches, Open Line, youth benches, support groups)
rows.explainer: The rest is research (published trials and protocols, the $75,000 grant to LSHTM) and Friendship Bench in a Box trainings abroad, which earn fees of their own (the 2024 report expects at least $200,000 from them by 2025); Friendship Bench in a Box trainings in Zimbabwe's new districts are part of the modelled programme. Neither research nor training abroad has a spending split or outcome data, so they are left out (Convention 12) and the result covers talk therapy in Zimbabwe only. Anchor: the US affiliate's programme fees for services ($209,378) and research grant ($75,000) are 12% of the group's programme spending (7% of all spending) at the best guess, and part of them may be Zimbabwe programme work. 0.9, range 0.8 to 1.

rows.label: Spending on talk therapy in Zimbabwe, 2024
rows.explainer: Programme spending in 2024 on the bench programme in Zimbabwe: problem-solving therapy by community health workers on benches at 385 clinics, the WhatsApp Open Line, the Youth Friendship Bench and the Circle Kubatana Tose peer groups. Research and the international trainings (about a tenth) are left out (Convention 12). 2024 is the latest year with financial filings (the US affiliate's Form 990; no 2025 return is filed yet) and reach for the same year.

Clients seen, 2024

source.title: Friendship Bench, Annual report 2024
source.page: p. 6 and the programme matrix, p. 9
source.quote: TOTAL NUMBER OF CLIENTS SEEN BY FRIENDSHIP BENCH IN 2024: 295,770

rows.explainer: Clients seen in 2024: 285,900 face to face on the benches (including implementing partners) and 9,870 on the WhatsApp Open Line (p. 6; the programme matrix on p. 9 shows 5,895 for the Open Line, and p. 19 gives 300 clinics where p. 6 gives 385; the total of 295,770 is the same in both). The charity's own count; routine data at the clinics have been unreliable in the past (the RE-AIM evaluation of the scale-up), so delivery goes into implementation_adj. 2025: 336,215.

rows.label: Follow-up sessions, 2024 (estimated from the quarterly reports)

source.title: Friendship Bench, Q1, Q2 and Q3 2024 impact reports (programme matrices) and Annual report 2024
source.page: Q1 2024 p. 5, Q2 2024 p. 5, Q3 2024 p. 5 (programme matrix); Annual report 2024 p. 9
source.quote: Q3 2024: # of Clients seen ... 76,087; # of Follow-up sessions ... 82,313
source.note: Q1 2024: 69,721 clients, 4,707 follow-ups (Drive id 11JxYcf8HFB9U6RRzlIXnSOjDMpRNyiTP); Q2: 71,388 and 75,256 (1rpPGQcpWhn-eRIBSHncfk-x09HXVtjVZ); Q3: 76,087 and 82,313 (1Tn-Yt4UVmPet18vFSkj5_AnCdaxPS5qp); annual report: 295,770 and 47,073.

rows.explainer: Sessions after the first. The charity's counts disagree: the 2024 annual report gives 47,073 for the year, less than its own first three quarters together (162,276 follow-ups for 217,196 clients). Best guess: the Q1–Q3 rate (0.747 a client) times the year's 295,770 clients, 220,980. Low: the annual report's 47,073. High: the Q2–Q3 rate (about 1.07 a client), about 316,000, the first quarter's 4,707 looking like a recording gap. The count's uncertainty is here; the shape of the dose-response is dose_response_exponent's.

rows.label: Friendship Bench trial: PHQ-9 difference at 6 months (points)

source.title: Chibanda et al. 2016, Effect of a primary care-based psychological intervention on symptoms of common mental disorders in Zimbabwe: a randomized clinical trial, JAMA 316(24):2618–2626
source.quote: nonprespecified continuous variables for the PHQ-9 scores (AMD, −6.36; 95% CI, −6.45 to −5.27

rows.explainer: 573 primary-care clients in Harare with common mental disorders (SSQ-14 ≥ 9), cluster-randomised: six sessions of problem-solving therapy on a bench by trained lay health workers plus an optional peer group, against enhanced usual care. Adjusted mean difference 6.36 PHQ-9 points at about six months (median 171 days). The printed interval (−6.45 to −5.27) is not centred on the estimate, so the range here is ±1.96 × 0.688 points, the standard error from the two arms' intervals in Table 2 (4.50, 3.95–5.05, against 11.01, 9.78–12.24). The PHQ-9 was not the prespecified primary outcome (the SSQ-14 was: −4.86, −5.63 to −4.10).

rows.label: Friendship Bench trial effect (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: PHQ-9 points into SDs at the site's one spread, @depression.phq9_sd.

rows.label: Standard error of the trial's PHQ-9 difference (points)

source.title: Chibanda et al. 2016, JAMA
source.quote: intervention 4.50 (95% CI, 3.95 to 5.05); control 11.01 (95% CI, 9.78 to 12.24)

rows.explainer: Worked: each arm's interval width ÷ 3.92 gives 0.281 and 0.628 points; their root sum of squares is 0.688. The intervals come from the cluster-adjusted model, so the clustering is in them. A spread used for the weights, so no range of its own.

rows.label: Standard error of the trial effect (SD)
Task-shared psychological treatment in low- and middle-income countries: pooled effect (SD)

source.title: Karyotaki et al. 2022, Association of task-shared psychological interventions with depression outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis, JAMA Psychiatry 79(5):430–443
source.quote: The 2-stage IPD-MA resulted in a g of 0.32 (95% CI, 0.18-0.46; P < .001) in favor of task-shared psychological interventions.

rows.explainer: Eleven trials, 4,145 participants, PHQ-9 after treatment, delivered by non-specialists (problem solving and behavioural activation in most), no sign of publication bias. The Friendship Bench trial is not among them. The conventional meta-analysis of all 13 eligible trials gives 0.48 (0.26–0.68); Cuijpers et al. 2018 find 1.10 for psychotherapy in non-Western countries overall, 0.73 after adjusting for publication bias and 0.51 in the trials at low risk of bias.

rows.label: Spread a new implementer faces around the pooled effect (SD)

source.title: Karyotaki et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry
source.quote: The PIs ranged from g = −0.12 to 0.76.

rows.explainer: From the prediction interval, which carries the between-trial spread: (0.76 − (−0.12)) ÷ 3.92 = 0.2245. A spread used for the weights, so no range of its own.

rows.label: Weight of the trial by precision alone
rows.explainer: The standard precision weight (templates.md, wellbeing): about 65% at the defaults. The weight used is the next row.

rows.label: Discount on the trial's precision weight for a trial unlike today's programme
rows.explainer: The trial is unlike today's programme in how it was delivered: a research team trained and supervised a few dozen lay health workers in 2014–2015, against 2,773 community health workers today, trained in short courses and supervised across ten provinces. Reference class: effects found in single trials shrink when programmes scale or move to new implementers (Vivalt 2020, Journal of the European Economic Association, on how far impact evaluations generalise; Bold et al. 2018, Journal of Public Economics, where a programme that worked under an NGO had no effect when the government ran it), and an effect four to five times the pooled one is the kind that shrinks most. 0.7, so the trial keeps about 45% of the weight instead of 65%; 1 (precision alone) at the high end, 0.4 at the low. The fewer sessions clients get today are not counted here but in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Weight on the Friendship Bench trial in the blend
rows.explainer: The precision weight, moved down by the ranged judgment above (templates.md, wellbeing).

rows.label: Effect of a full course, blended (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: The trial and the literature blended (templates.md, wellbeing): about 0.86 SD at the defaults, 0.57 times the trial's 1.51. The trial measured at about six months, the meta-analysis just after treatment; both are taken as the effect at the end of treatment.

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded
rows.explainer: Years until the effect has faded to zero, linearly. Anchors: the Friendship Bench trial still shows its full effect at six months, and the Healthy Activity Programme (lay counsellors, India; Weobong et al. 2017, PLoS Medicine) kept its gains from 3 to 12 months, so a linear fade reaching zero before about 2.5 years would contradict them (at 2.5 years the effect is 80% of its start at six months, 60% at a year). The low end, 1.5, allows the decay these follow-ups can't see in a programme giving fewer sessions; the high end, 4, a plateau after a year. No trial of this kind follows clients for several years with a control group.

rows.label: Implied decay of the effect (SDs per year)
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the decay rates reported in follow-up studies.

rows.label: Discount rate, continuous
rows.explainer: The shared yearly rate as a continuous rate, so the effect can be discounted smoothly as it fades.

rows.label: Discount factor for the fading effect
rows.formula: if(continuous_discount_rate > 0, (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years - 1 + exp(-(continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years))) / (0.5 * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years) * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years)), 1)
rows.explainer: Present value of the triangle (linear fade to zero) at the shared rate, as a share of its undiscounted area; as in the HLI models.

rows.label: Total effect per person (SD-years, discounted)
rows.explainer: Area of the triangle: linear decay from the initial effect to zero, discounted.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person treated
rows.explainer: SD-years into WELLBYs at the site's one rate (@wellby_factors). The WELLBY slider then puts WELLBYs into healthy years, calibrated so a year of depression is worth the same here as through the GBD weights (@depression); never convert depression into DALYs inside this model.

rows.label: Household size
rows.explainer: The site's household size for Zimbabwe (facts/household_size.json, DHS 2015, 4.1): clients are urban and rural primary-care users across all ten provinces, so the national figure.

rows.label: Household multiplier (recipient plus spillovers)
rows.explainer: Each other household member gains the site's one share of the recipient's effect (HLI's, @wellby_factors).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Two parts left after the blend: (1) self-report and response bias on an interviewer-administered PHQ-9, 0.9 (both trial and meta-analysis rely on it; assessors were blinded in most trials); (2) whether a client seen has the distress the trial treated: the programme gives therapy to those above the SSQ-14 cut-off "and/or" who wish to receive it (RE-AIM 2022); 2,990 of 3,009 clients in the 2025 follow-up cohort with paired scores were symptomatic (99%), and 966 of the 1,003 reached from a random sample of Q3 2024 clients (96%, Q3 2024 impact report p. 6), but in the 2007 pilot only 42% of bench visitors scored above the cut-off, and the trial enrolled screened clients (SSQ-14 ≥ 9), while clients at scale include walk-ins with milder distress, who have less to gain: 0.9, range 0.45 to 1. Product 0.8, range 0.4 to 1. Publication bias is not adjusted again (the meta-analysis found none) and the trial's own size is handled by its weight. After the blend, this and implementation_adj, a client seen gets about 0.33 SD, 0.22 times the trial's effect.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the effects are against control arms with enhanced usual care (nurse assessment, brief counselling, antidepressants offered), which is what clients would get without the bench; Zimbabwe has few other psychological services outside the bench. Down to 0.9 for other services reaching some clients.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Most benches are run by community health workers employed by city health departments and the Ministry of Health with a basic salary (RE-AIM evaluation of the scale-up), at government clinics, and the Ministry is taking the programme over (annual report 2024, p. 10). Anchor, built from the model's own numbers: 295,770 first sessions and about 221,000 follow-ups at 30–45 minutes (the trial's length) are about 320,000 hours, some 115 hours a year per health worker (about 6% of full time); with screening, mobilisation and support-group work perhaps twice that, about $0.3 million a year at $50–100 a month, against Friendship Bench's $3.6 million. Clinic space, nurses' referrals, government supervisors' time and implementing partners' benches (7,382 of 295,770 clients in the 2024 programme matrix) add some more: 0.9, range 0.7 to 0.97.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: How the effect grows with sessions (exponent of the dose share)
rows.explainer: The share of a full course's effect is (sessions received ÷ the trial's sessions) to this power: 1 is proportional, below 1 front-loaded. Anchors: the 2011 Friendship Bench pilot found the fall in SSQ-14 scores "proportional to the number of sessions attended" (its adjusted table, which only covers 3 to 6 sessions, even shows later sessions adding more), which sets the high end, 1.2. Single-session interventions reach g = 0.32 in a meta-analysis of 50 trials (Schleider & Weisz 2017, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry; 0.21 for depression), about what a full course of task-shared therapy reaches in the meta-analysis used here (0.32), and the classic dose-effect curve flattens as sessions add up (Howard et al. 1986): these set the low end, 0.35. 0.7 best: at 1.75 sessions of 5, about half a full course.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The share of a full course's effect a client seen gets: sessions per client seen (about 1.75 in 2024; the count is uncertain, see follow_up_sessions) over the trial's median of 5, to the power dose_response_exponent. About 0.48 at the defaults. Whether a client seen has the distress treated at all is asked once, in evidence_adj. Check: the charity's own six-week follow-up finds 85% recovery (2025; 82% in 2024), but only among the 22% of a sampled cohort with paired scores, those who could be reached, and without a control group (the trial's controls improved too), so it doesn't move the dose share.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Suicides per 100,000 men aged 15–49 a year, Zimbabwe, 2023

source.title: WHO, Global Health Estimates 2023 summary tables (September 2026): deaths by cause, age and sex, by country
source.page: Sheets '15-29' and '30-49', column ZWE, rows 'Males: Population ('000)' and 'Males: 1610 Self-harm'

rows.label: Share of clients who are women

source.title: Friendship Bench, Annual report 2025
source.quote: Our overall FB reach indicates that we serve 64% of women

rows.explainer: 2025 figure; 2024's split is not published.

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of the people treated (before their depression)
rows.explainer: The clients' sex mix (64% women) over WHO's rates for ages 15–49.

rows.label: Relative risk of suicide for people with the distress treated
rows.explainer: Depression is among the disorders with the highest suicide risk (Chesney, Goodwin & Fazel 2014, World Psychiatry 13(2):153, a meta-review), many times the general population's for major depression; clients of the bench mostly have mild to moderate depression or anxiety (the trial excluded those at high suicide risk, the 2011 pilot 8% of those screened), so 5, range 2.5 to 15. Clients without the distress are counted in evidence_adj, not here.

rows.label: Share of the excess suicide risk removed at the end of treatment
rows.explainer: In the trial, suicidal ideation at follow-up was 2.3% against 12.3% in the control arm; ideation is far more common than suicide and no trial of brief therapy has measured suicides. 20%, range 5% to 40%, applied to a full course (implementation_adj scales it like the WELLBYs).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person treated (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Suicides averted per person given a full course, by the site's recipe (templates.md, wellbeing): the clients' yearly suicide rate × (relative risk − 1) × the share of the excess removed, over the effect's years as it fades and discounted like the WELLBYs.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weight for ages 15–49 (the trial's clients averaged about 33 years), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Deaths averted, in units of value
Deaths averted, in WELLBYs (cancelled by the unit's conversion)
rows.explainer: The one row that puts units of value into WELLBYs; the WELLBY unit's conversion multiplies it back, so the deaths count exactly their shared value at any WELLBY rate.
